>one of the things that has been bothering me from critiques that I saw so far is the strong emphasis on the historical inaccuracies in the movie

I hate that it's become a meme where people mention the historical inaccuracies whenever they want to criticize Braveheart. It's like they missed the very first thing said in the movie, where it is admitted that history books will not tell the same story as what we see in this film:

> I shall tell you of William Wallace. Historians from England will say I am a liar, but history is written by those who have hanged heroes.

>Depending on your preference. You might call this movie a classic. But for me personally, I would not go that far i just think it was just an excellent movie witha perfect structue 

This is not a very r/TrueFilm kind of movie, but I'm not only going to call it a classic, I'm going to abuse a Pederewski quote for this:

>The greatest accomplishment of any artist in any form of human endeavour whatsoever.

I very recently rewatched this favourite of mine, in hard times, and I was repeatedly astounded by its simple granduer. Many a film - by the likes of Lean, Jackson or Scott - have outdone it for the sheer number of moving parts, but few have matched its emotional honesty, and its focus on visual storytelling.

I feel like when we say "Visual storytelling" we often basically devolve it to montage and painting a mood: so slow motion and drenched colour means sad and that kind of stuff. Braveheart's visual storytelling is not like that: there are sequences of ten to fifteen minutes in a row, where nary a word is spoken, and they're not about trekking montages of setting a mood, but they actually forward the plot.

The directorial choices continually bewilder me. There's a confrontation here between Wallace, the Council and Robert the Bruce, just before the Battle of Falkirk. First thing, Wallace has an entrance as showstopping as anything, partially because Gibson (as the director) has him enter right in the middle of another character giving dialogue. Then, when Wallace goes into a one-on-one discussion with The Bruce, we start with a wideshot in which the nobles are in the shot. Then we punch in closer, but Gibson cunningly keeps the biggest closeup to the most dramatic moment later in the dialogue. Its simple, and its brilliant.

Ontop of all of that, to have this film - which is Gibson's sophomoric directorial effort - be so sure-handed is nothing short of a minor miracle. Its in the pacing: I feel like most directors, given this material, would be a little bit of a rush to get to Stirling. But Gibson isn't: he makes you sit and wait patiently for it. And its not done in a David Lean-like largesse, but just as self-assured: "No, dear audience, this is important, and you will sit hear and enjoy this shot, and now appreciate this beat, and you will wait."

If that's a minor miracle, the pulling off of the battles is as great a miracle as anything described in any biblical tale: that the film didn't implode here defies belief. These battles have been used as a template and inspiration for just about any large-scale ground battle filmed since 1995, but its scarcely if ever been better: the build-up is so drawn-out, it wouldn't feel out of place in a Sergio Leone film, and the combination of staccato cutting, foreground acton, copious gore effects and smart choices of lenses from John Toll all create a most visceral experience.

Performances are uniformally excellent, especially an outstanding, hillarious David O'Hara. The look of the film is gorgeous: Gibson and Toll's decision to NOT wait to magic hours and sunny days gave the film a look that may be less pretty than Gladiator or Ryan's Daughter, but has much more atmosphere: There are movies that take place in icy tundras where you don't feel the cold as palpably as you do here.

And I find the ending incredibly unlifting, moving and glorious: its a cinematic Verklarung. No movie that I've ever seen before or since leaves me with this feeling of walking on air after its over. 

Sublime from one end to the other.

Every period piece is fundamentally inaccurate and people (hopefully) know that, but I think this one causes dissonance for a lot of people. It plays itself super straight and earnestly with the plot and style of like, [America: the Motion Picture](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hu0O-q7Kf2k) or something.
I've actually never seen the film in question, but I think this gets at an interesting question about historical fiction's obligation -- or lack thereof -- to historical reality.

>It plays itself super straight and earnestly with the plot and style of like

I don't think you can say it does that when the movie starts by saying it's deviating from history books.

You have the most bizarre, arbitrary scoring system I have ever seen. I don't see a reason for it to be like that at all.

I agree with you about the historical inaccuracy aspects of thngs though. I feel that way about any retelling, historical or contemporary.
I know. You just said that. It doesn't have anything to do with my point.

I'm all for not being historically accurate.  Braveheart is basically a fantasy film.  There is very little that has to do with the real story.  

That is fine, but you are wrong to say the movie doesn't claim to be based on a true story.  (Well it is "based" on a true story).  In the beginning the narrator literally says; "I shall tell you of William Wallace. Historians from England will say I am a liar, but history is written by those who have hanged heroes."  

For a fantasy movie based on a real person, this line is a really bad look.  Imagine if they tried to tell you something like that at the beginning of Abraham Lincoln Vampire Hunter?

It literally is advertising the opposite though:  "I shall tell you of William Wallace. Historians from England will say I am a liar, but history is written by those who have hanged heroes."  

It is telling you, "don't listen to historians, we have the true history right here."

>I know. You just said that.

Sorry, I felt like you responded without acknowledging what I said and found it confusing.

>It's very serious, grim, and sincere despite the ridiculous overtones.

hmm Yeah, I can understand this as a criticism in itself, but I just don't think that has much to do with historical accuracy. It's too excessive/over-the-top for how seriously it takes itself. I'm not sure I agree, but that's definitely valid.

hmmm interesting point , i never really pay any attention to introductory narration but upon further review you are right , it did claim and that is absolutely a bad look and would only worsen the argument for mel gibson

>It literally is advertising the opposite though

What? No, it literally says history books are incorrect. Not the opposite of what I said (ie. that it will deviate from history books), but exactly what I said.

I’d like to think OP has an entire binder of documentation describing the point systems here - having some elements on the standard 5 or 10 point system and then other elements randomly on a 3 or 6 point system. It reminds me of something a hardcore D&D dungeon master would come up with. 


Maybe it’s not superfluous, maybe OP has actually come up with the most refined film rating system the world has ever seen. And here we all are, mocking them, ignorant of the fact that we are trapped in Platonic cave of thumbs and stars.

my scoring system is for sure overwhelming but comprehensive to me and to the movies i rate, i didn't start the scoring system with this many points initially, each point has a story behind it from a movie i watched that had something in it that deserved a point and 2 years in now I'm re-rating all of my old rated movies because my current scoring system seems to be very efficient, especially for recommendation engines.  it's a deliberate breakdown of crucial elements in storytelling. Uniqueness, structure, tension, dialogue.  They're carefully chosen because they matter in evaluating a movie. Maybe it's not for everyone, especially those who like things simple. But this system caters to those who appreciate a nuanced evaluation. It's not about being nice; it's about being thorough.
well said ,  nice breakdown of the cinematography of the movie, it was sure one of the best in its period
well said ,  nice breakdown of the cinematography of the movie, it was sure one of the best in its period

What will you do if you come across a movie you like but doesn't fit into your scoring system? As in a movie that is not about character and/or plot. Will it break your system or will you decide you must not actually like it?
No, it's been scientifically determined that "camera angles and movement" make up exactly 3% of a movie's overall quality.

Great question! Let's unravel this.

Of course, personal preference matters, and my scoring system isn't a cold, technical machine. Personal preference is baked right in. Check out "Emotional Connection" and "Ending" – they're like my emotional barometers. If I'm into a movie, those scores show it, no doubt. Other criteria are also subjective, like the movie dialogue and pacing/suspense. We are not machines, and even the most objective criteria can become subjective when adding a human element into the mix. That's what I'm always doing. I'm not a technical freak who analyzes everything with precision, and my ratings are not objective by any chance. You could use the same system and get completely different results because you will  be biased with your own subjective believes , we don't research each movie after watching it to identify common flaws and then rate based on them. That is never the case.

Check out categories like "Setting" and "Pacing & Suspense." It's not a one-note show about characters and plot. A killer setting or suspenseful pacing can crank up the score, even if the plot takes a back seat. Movies aren't clones, and my scoring system gets that. It's not a one-size-fits-all deal. Each movie gets its fair shake based on what it brings to the table.

So, the idea that my system crumbles if I like a movie that's not all about characters and plot? Nah, it's designed to groove with the diversity of movies and my personal tastes.

What's your vibe on that?

Yeah that part really doesn't sit right with me.  Had they not included it I would have forgiven it and just treated it like a King Arthur movie.  

Mel Gibson has been better at saying it was a fantasy, but Randall Wallace the writer has kind of danced around it instead of just saying; "look guys it is a fantasy and we weren't making a historical film."
Lol that is what I said.  It says "the history books are wrong, we have the real story" as they tell a completely different story than what actually happened.
Right, but you could say the same about something like Game of Thrones.  Obviously it takes itself very seriously even though it is obviously a fantasy that takes place on another world.

If i could give you any advice is to have shorter answers. You always write this complicated short stories and there's just no way someone is reading all of it. Especially when we are talking about some trivial shit like movie scoring criteria.

Imagine, indeed, a binder thicker than the plot twists in a Christopher Nolan film, detailing the intricate dance of points on a scale known only to the chosen few.

Perhaps, in the spirit of jest about D&D dungeon masters, imagine a secret guild of Film Rating Wizards. Your humble OP, adorned in a cape fashioned from film reel strips, guides the enchanting manual, orchestrating points – some on a 3, others on a 6. Just a bit of cinematic chaos to keep the audience on their toes.

My gues would be is that it was intended to be based on true story at first but when they faced criticism from the historians they changed the narrative  , but it absolutely doesn't help if they have an introductory narration that claim otherwise
sorry for the long answers .  i was just clarifying a misunderstanding about a rating system that i invested alot of time to make it
Agreed my man.  Appreciate your review.  I know I nitpicked one thing you said, but overall appreciate your thoughtful essay.

Interesting, I always interpreted it the opposite way, as basically a tell that the film isn’t going to be historically accurate and a way to quickly wash their hands of any complaints about inaccuracy

I get what you're saying but i disagree. I think "this story is different than history books" presents itself as fiction. You have to believe the filmmakers know more about history than historians to think otherwise, which no reasonable person would think.

I don't think I could. Game of Thrones is a grimdark fantasy world that looks the part. The characters are just as dingy inside and out.

Braveheart plays out like a tragic chivalric romance (even with the mooning) with the style of pulp fantasy. I think the perception of a "knight" is a little too obvious for some people to overlook.
